deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page sets up a Lagrangian / Hamilton-principle model of point charges (mass m, charge ε, position x=(x,y,z)) moving through an elastic medium, the ether, whose displacement field is (ξ,η,ζ). The particles couple linearly to the ether displacement. Riemann derives the field equation and the particle equation. He then tries to recast the dynamics as a quadratic form in the accelerations, in the spirit of Gauss's principle of least constraint.

(1) Lagrangian (top line). In modern notation he writes
2(T+U) = Σ_particles m|ẋ|² + 2ε ẋ·ξ(x,t) + ∫dS [ a|∂_tξ|² + b Σ_{i,k}(∂ξ_i/∂x_k)² + (c−b)(∇·ξ)² ].
U is evidently 'minus potential energy'. For the field equation that follows to have the wave (not anti-wave) sign, the b and (c−b) terms must enter with the opposite sign to a|ξ_t|²; that is my reading. The coupling 2ε ẋ·ξ is exactly the modern 2q v·A interaction, with the ether displacement playing the role of the vector potential A.

(2) Principle. ∫(T+U)dt = Min. This is Hamilton's principle, stationarity of the action.

(3) Field equation, from varying ξ. The particle term becomes a distributed source ε ẋ δ(r−x(t)), written by Riemann as ε dx/(dt dS), i.e. charge velocity per volume element dS. The result is
a ∂²ξ/∂t² = b Δξ + (c−b) ∂(∇·ξ)/∂x − ε (dx/dt)/dS,
and similarly for η, ζ. This is the Navier–Lamé equation of an isotropic elastic solid with a current-density source. b is the shear (transverse) stiffness and c the longitudinal stiffness; transverse waves travel at √(b/a) and longitudinal ones at √(c/a).

My remark: in temporal gauge (φ=0) Maxwell's equations read A_tt = −c_L² curl curl A + j = c_L²(ΔA − ∇∇·A) + j. This coincides with Riemann's equation exactly when c=0, i.e. a medium with no longitudinal stiffness (the later Kelvin 'labile ether'). Riemann keeps c general.

(4) General Lagrangian mechanics. Take T = Σ a_{ιι'} x'_ι x'_{ι'} + … (the crossed continuation presumably holds the linear-in-velocity terms). Then
δ∫(T−U)dt = Σ∫(∂T/∂x'_ι δx'_ι + ∂(T−U)/∂x_ι δx_ι)dt.
Integrating by parts gives the boundary term [∂T/∂x'_ι δx_ι] plus ∫δx_ι(−d/dt ∂T/∂x'_ι + ∂(T−U)/∂x_ι)dt. Hence the Euler–Lagrange equations
d/dt(∂T/∂x'_ι) = ∂(T−U)/∂x_ι.

(5) Particle equation. Apply (4) to T ⊃ ½m|ẋ|² + ε ẋ·ξ(x,t).
- The first attempt, m(ẍ + ε dξ/dt) = ε Σ ∂ξ_ι/∂x ẋ_ι + …, wrongly multiplies the ε-term by m and is struck.
- The corrected form is
m ẍ + ε( ∂ξ/∂t + Σ_ι (∂ξ/∂x_ι − ∂ξ_ι/∂x) ẋ_ι ) = 0.
- This uses dξ/dt = ∂_tξ + (ẋ·∇)ξ along the trajectory.
- In vector form it reads m ẍ = −ε ∂_tξ + ε ẋ × (∇×ξ).
- So it is the Lorentz force with E = −∂_tA, B = curl A and A ≡ ξ (no scalar potential).

(6) Lower half: least-constraint form. Riemann multiplies the bracket (m ẍ + ε(...)) by 2ẍ dt² and forms
dt²[ m(ẍ)² + 2ε(∂_tξ + Σ(∂ξ/∂x_ι − ∂ξ_ι/∂x)ẋ_ι)·ẍ ] + … + 2U dS.
It is then rewritten as m ẍ² + 2ε(dξ/dt·ẍ − d²ξ/dt²·ẋ)dt² (the last factor partly struck).
To this he adds field contributions:
- a(∂²ξ/∂t²)² dt²;
- the derivative of b(∂ξ/∂x)², namely 2b ∂ξ/∂x ∂³ξ/∂x∂t²;
- the identity ∂ξ/∂t · d(∂ξ/∂t)/dt dt² = ½ d(∂ξ/∂t)² dt;
- a convective term 2a ∂_tξ ∂²ξ/∂t∂x_ι ẍ_ι dt² (my interpretation: from differentiating along the particle path).

Minimising the quadratic form m ẍ² + 2εF·ẍ over ẍ gives m ẍ + εF = 0, i.e. equation (5). The aim is evidently a Gauss/Gibbs–Appell type 'Zwang' functional for the coupled particle–ether system, with the field terms handled by splitting off total time differentials. This part is unfinished and heavily corrected; no final result is stated.
errors: Sign bookkeeping is inconsistent. The functional is called 2(T+U) and ∫(T+U)dt is minimised, yet the Euler–Lagrange step uses T−U. With all terms of the top line positive, varying ξ gives a ξ_tt = −bΔξ − …. The written wave equation requires the b,(c−b) terms to carry the opposite sign to aξ_t², i.e. U is minus the elastic energy.

The sign of the source term −ε ẋ/dS depends on the same convention. If the elastic terms enter with the opposite sign and the coupling with +2ε, variation gives +ε ẋ δ. So the minus sign is either a slip or an implicit convention.
'Min.': Hamilton's principle gives stationarity, not in general a minimum (standard 19th-century usage, not a real error).
The first particle equation m(d²x/dt² + ε dξ/dt) wrongly puts the ε-term inside the factor m. Riemann struck it and corrected it to m d²x/dt² + ε(...).
In the least-constraint section the line with −d²ξ/dt²·dx/dt is not dimensionally consistent with the preceding line. It is partly crossed out and the computation is left incomplete.

results.what: Lagrangian for charged mass points coupled linearly (ε v·ξ) to an elastic ether displacement, plus isotropic elastic field energy; joint Hamilton principle for particles and field
results.modern_name: Coupled particle–field action (minimal coupling q v·A) with an elastic-solid ether
results.usually_credited_to: Velocity-dependent electrodynamic potentials: Weber 1846, Neumann 1845–48. Lagrangian field theory of electromagnetism: Maxwell 1865/1873. Full particle+field action: Larmor 1900, Schwarzschild 1903.

results.what: Field equation a ξ_tt = bΔξ + (c−b)∇(∇·ξ) − ε v δ (current-sourced elastic wave equation)
results.modern_name: Navier–Lamé equation with source; equals the temporal-gauge Maxwell equation for A when c=0
results.usually_credited_to: Navier 1821, Cauchy, Lamé; sourced vector wave equation for A: Lorenz 1867, Maxwell 1865

results.what: Euler–Lagrange equations via integration by parts of δ∫(T−U)dt
Particle equation m ẍ + ε(∂_tξ + Σ(∂ξ/∂x_ι − ∂ξ_ι/∂x)ẋ_ι) = 0, i.e. m ẍ = ε(−∂_tξ + v×curl ξ)
results.modern_name: Lorentz force derived from the vector-potential Lagrangian ½mv² + q v·A
results.usually_credited_to: Maxwell 1865 (electromotive force v×B − ∂A/∂t); Heaviside 1889; Lorentz 1892/95; Lagrangian derivation standard after Schwarzschild 1903

results.what: Attempt to express the dynamics as a quadratic form in accelerations to be minimised (m ẍ² + 2εF·ẍ + field terms)
results.modern_name: Gauss's principle of least constraint / Gibbs–Appell acceleration function

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's ether speculations and his 1858 retarded-potential electrodynamics are known. However, a worked Lagrangian in which charges couple to an elastic ether exactly through ε v·ξ, giving the full Lorentz force (−∂_tA plus v×curl A) and a current-sourced vector wave equation, is a notable unpublished detail. Such a model anticipates Maxwell–Larmor–Schwarzschild style particle–field action principles. It is not a finished theory: there is no scalar potential, c is not set to 0, and the Gauss-principle part is incomplete. Hence a moderate score.

checkable.sympy: t=symbols('t'); m,e=symbols('m e'); x,y,z=[Function(n)(t) for n in 'xyz']; X,Y,Z,T=symbols('X Y Z T'); A=[Function(n)(X,Y,Z,T) for n in ('A1','A2','A3')]; sub={X:x,Y:y,Z:z,T:t}; L=m/2*(x.diff(t)**2+y.diff(t)**2+z.diff(t)**2)+e*sum(Ai.subs(sub)*qi.diff(t) for Ai,qi in zip(A,[x,y,z])); EL=diff(L.diff(x.diff(t)),t)-L.diff(x)
checkable.asserts: Euler–Lagrange for x: EL equals m*x'' + e*(dA1/dT + Σ_ι (dA1/dX_ι − dA_ι/dX) x_ι'), Riemann's corrected particle equation.

checkable.sympy: v=Matrix(symbols('v1 v2 v3')); X=symbols('X1 X2 X3'); A=Matrix([Function('A%d'%i)(*X) for i in (1,2,3)]); curl=Matrix([A[2].diff(X[1])-A[1].diff(X[2]),A[0].diff(X[2])-A[2].diff(X[0]),A[1].diff(X[0])-A[0].diff(X[1])]); lhs=v.cross(curl)[0]; rhs=sum((A[i].diff(X[0])-A[0].diff(X[i]))*v[i] for i in range(3)); simplify(lhs-rhs)==0
checkable.asserts: Σ_ι(∂ξ_ι/∂x − ∂ξ/∂x_ι)ẋ_ι equals the x-component of v×curl ξ, i.e. the magnetic Lorentz term.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c=symbols('a b c'); X=symbols('X1 X2 X3'); t=symbols('t'); xi=[Function('xi%d'%i)(*X,t) for i in range(3)]; div=sum(xi[i].diff(X[i]) for i in range(3)); Lden=Rational(1,2)*(a*sum(f.diff(t)**2 for f in xi)-b*sum(xi[i].diff(X[k])**2 for i in range(3) for k in range(3))-(c-b)*div**2); from sympy.calculus.euler import euler_equations; euler_equations(Lden,xi,[*X,t])[0]
checkable.asserts: With the elastic terms of opposite sign to the kinetic term, the field equation is a*xi_tt = b*Laplacian(xi) + (c-b)*d(div xi)/dx (source-free part of Riemann's equation).

checkable.sympy: b=symbols('b'); X=symbols('X1 X2 X3'); A=Matrix([Function('A%d'%i)(*X) for i in (1,2,3)]); curl=lambda F: Matrix([F[2].diff(X[1])-F[1].diff(X[2]),F[0].diff(X[2])-F[2].diff(X[0]),F[1].diff(X[0])-F[0].diff(X[1])]); div=sum(A[i].diff(X[i]) for i in range(3)); lap=Matrix([sum(A[j].diff(X[i],2) for i in range(3)) for j in range(3)]); grad=Matrix([div.diff(X[i]) for i in range(3)]); simplify(-b*curl(curl(A)) - (b*lap+(0-b)*grad))==zeros(3,1)
checkable.asserts: For c=0, bΔξ + (c−b)∇(∇·ξ) = −b curl curl ξ, so Riemann's field equation becomes the temporal-gauge Maxwell equation for A.
Minimising the acceleration form m*acc^2 + 2*e*F*acc gives acc = -e*F/m, recovering the equation of motion (least-constraint step).
d(∂ξ/∂t)²/dt = 2 ∂ξ/∂t ∂²ξ/∂t², the total-differential identity used at the bottom of the page.

transcription_corrections: Line 'm(d²x/dt² + ε dξ/dt) = ε Σ ∂x_ι/∂x dx_ι/dt': the numerator is ∂ξ_ι/∂x (ether displacement component), not ∂x_ι/∂x.
First line: the leading symbol is m (overwritten/blotted, not deleted), so the term is m Σ(dx/dt)².
Source term in the field equation: read as ε dx/(dt dS), i.e. charge velocity per volume element dS.
In the Euler–Lagrange integration-by-parts line, the illegible bracket should be −d/dt(∂T/∂x'_ι), consistent with the next line.
'+2U dS' at the end of the long dt² line: probably 2U dS (field potential per volume element); legibility uncertain.
